meta.regime: Two central banks moved this board with their own words rather than with data, and in the same direction: toward later. The Fed's October 27-28 hike was repriced from 69-73% before Tuesday's core PCE to 47.1% on CME and about 35% on Kalshi and Polymarket, after John Williams said there is 'no urgency' - but the cumulative pricing through December 9 is unchanged at roughly 90% for at least one more 25bp move, so what shifted is timing, not direction. Hours later the BoJ's Summary of Opinions from the September meeting damped bets on a back-to-back October hike, and the yen became the worst G10 performer at -0.55%, with USD/JPY at 158.279. The second fact is what did not continue: yesterday's energy collapse has stalled. WTI is 89.046 and still falling, but German gas is +4.09% in a session, UK gas is back to 182.17 GBp/thm from 175.26, and Brent is +1.28% on the month.
meta.nextBigEvent: US payrolls on Friday October 2 at 12:30Z, forecast 89K against 162K with unemployment 4.1% and earnings 0.3%. With October now a minority call, this print decides whether December stays the near-certainty it is priced as - and the funding deal signed for FY2027 means the release is not at risk.

dailyRead: Nothing in the data did the work today - two central banks did it with their own words, and both of them said later rather than no. Start with the Fed, because it is the larger of the two. Tuesday's core PCE at 0.2% m/m against 0.3% forecast, with the y/y rate at 3.0% against a 3.3% forecast and headline at 3.4% against 3.7% expected, was already on this page. What has happened since is the repricing, and it is severe at the front: CME FedWatch now puts the October 27-28 hike at 47.1% with a hold at 52.9%, one read has it as low as 37%, and Kalshi and Polymarket are near 35%, against the 69-73% this page carried before the print. John Williams supplied the words, pushing back on an imminent follow-up and saying there is 'no urgency' after September's move. But read the rest of the curve before cutting the dollar again, because this is the part the headlines missed: the probability of the funds rate being unchanged through December 9 is only about 10%, with 51.8% priced for a cumulative 25bp and 38.2% for a cumulative 50bp. The market has not stopped expecting Fed tightening - it has moved it one meeting to the right. Williams himself still sees one more hike later this year; Goolsbee said inflation staying above target for five and a half years is 'playing with fire'; sixteen of eighteen officials in the September SEP see at least one more 25bp move this year with four penciling in two; and the SEP median remains 4.1% for year-end against a 4.00% upper bound today. So the dollar holds +2 rather than falling to +1, and the tape agrees in a way that is hard to argue with - DXY rose 0.18% to 101.651 on the day the October hike was priced out, it is +2.06% on the month, and the US ten-year rose to 5.2820 for a real yield near 2.88%. A currency that gains while its central bank is repriced dovish is being held for carry and for the absence of alternatives, which is exactly what the rest of this board now provides. The yen is the day's genuine score change and the one this page has to own, because yesterday it was raised to +2. The BoJ published its Summary of Opinions from the September 17-18 meeting at 23:50Z, and the market read it as a refusal rather than a signal: the yen fell as much as 0.55% to 158.279 and was the worst G10 performer, with investors cutting bets on a back-to-back hike on October 30. Be precise about what the Summary actually contained, because the structural case is not what broke. Members described a shift in the phase of policy from lifting inflation to stabilising it around 2%; one said that 'if signs of an upward deviation in prices are observed, the Bank will need to accelerate the pace of rate hikes'; most favoured further increases after September's move to 1.25%, a 31-year high. A Cabinet Office representative urged the Bank to examine carefully the cumulative effects of past hikes, and Asada and Sato remain the two dissenters. The Tankan the same morning pointed the same way, with large-manufacturer sentiment up for a sixth consecutive quarter to plus 24 from plus 22 - though it missed the plus 25 expected. So Japan's direction is intact and its wage data at 4.7% y/y is still the only credible second-round mechanism on this board. What is gone is the October catalyst that justified the second point, and a currency whose next move has been pushed from four weeks away to twelve cannot hold +2 while it is the worst performer in its peer group. JPY goes to +1. Sterling is the mirror image, and here the honest statement is that yesterday's cut to 0 over-extrapolated a single session of energy relief. The cut rested on two legs: that Bailey made the current stance explicitly conditional on high energy, and that both prices the Bank named on September 14 - Brent at 106 dollars and UK gas at 207 GBp/therm - had retreated. The second leg has partially reversed inside a day. UK gas is 182.17 GBp/thm against the 175.26 this page quoted yesterday, and it is now +0.01% on the month, not falling; German gas rose 4.09% in a single session; Brent at 96.857 is +1.28% on the month. On top of that the UK delivered the only positive growth revision on the board, with Q2 GDP lifted to 1.4% y/y, sterling rallied on it, and the UK ten-year at 5.4148 is now the highest of the majors, above Australia's 5.3920. Three MPC members already vote for 4.00%, and Breeden and Lombardelli have been reported moving closer to joining them. Against that, the Reuters-poll asymmetry this page named is still real - roughly 80% is priced for November 5 while about one in eight economists expected a hike - which is why sterling goes to +1 and not back to +2. The consequence is that two of yesterday's headline trades are withdrawn rather than reversed, and they should be named plainly: EUR/GBP, flipped LONG yesterday at 0.85668, has fallen to 0.85420 and goes to RANGE because the scores are now level at +1 each; GBP/JPY, flipped SHORT yesterday at 207.871, has risen to 209.704 and goes to RANGE for the same arithmetic reason. Withdrawing a call that has been overtaken is cheaper than chasing it in the other direction. The euro holds +1 on a case that is entirely relative and was built to be. German CPI accelerated to 3.3% from 2.9% and Friday's euro-area flash is forecast at 3.7% from 3.2%, but Lagarde has pre-announced that the ECB does not react to energy in either direction, so a hot print is a growth negative rather than a policy positive, negotiated wages are still 2.44% and decelerating, and the October 29 hike from a 2.50% deposit rate is already a measured base case. EUR/USD at 1.13173 is -2.34% on the month, which is what a passive reaction function looks like when everyone else repositions around it. Canada stays -1 and is unchanged in every particular: July GDP at 0.0% m/m, the only contracting PMIs on this board at 46.8 services and 47.8 composite, core CPI at 2.4% and headline m/m at -0.1%, with the BoC on hold at 2.25% into October 28. USD/CAD at 1.42472 is +2.93% on the month and remains the cleanest three-point gap on the page. Australia holds 0 - the highest policy rate here at 4.60% and a 5.3920 ten-year against unemployment rising to 4.6%, GDP decelerating to 2.1% and an energy-import story that has stopped helping either way. New Zealand holds -1 as the worst major of the month at -3.94%, with business confidence down to 51.9 from 53.7 and building permits to 3,339 from 3,487, and a Bank that has already framed Q2's 4.1% as fuel-driven. Switzerland stays -2 and remains the cleanest short leg on this board: zero per cent since mid-2025, core at 0.4%, wages at 0.4%, a 0.5690 ten-year, and a haven bid that has now failed on escalation days and de-escalation days alike. CPI at 06:30Z this morning and Schlegel at 15:30Z are both still ahead. Metals told a small story worth hearing: gold at 4182.57 is +0.60% but gave back a larger early rally as the ten-year rose and the dollar firmed, which is a soft tell on a day its own inflation print should have paid it, and silver at 61.246 outperformed it at +1.39%, reversing the direction of the decoupling this page flagged yesterday - so the silver short is withdrawn to RANGE. Copper is flat at 6.5541 into a Chinese Golden Week that started today. Both European indices fell, and the banks that are EU50's heaviest sector fell hardest at -1.13% to 310.74 even with a steepening curve, which is why EU50 is a RANGE rather than a long despite being +10.80% YTD against the DAX's +2.81% - and GER40 flips SHORT on a 4.09% single-session jump in German gas into a hawkish October 29 ECB. Practical read: USD/CHF and USD/CAD are the high-conviction tickets, CHF/JPY stays the cleanest cross short on the board at a three-point gap with carry in its favour, DXY flips back to LONG now that the yen no longer ties the dollar, and Friday's 89K payroll is the gate on every dollar leg.

USD.when: December 9 is now the live meeting rather than October 27-28. CME FedWatch puts October at 47.1% against a 52.9% hold, with one read at 37% and Kalshi and Polymarket near 35%, down from 69-73% before Tuesday's core PCE. Cumulative pricing through December 9 is unchanged: about 10% for no move at all, 51.8% for 25bp and 38.2% for 50bp. Payrolls on Friday October 2 is the gate
USD.note: TE re-verified: the upper bound of the fed funds target range is 4.00%, raised from 3.75% on September 16 in a unanimous decision - the first increase since 2023. TE's own summary of that meeting: 16 of 18 officials see the possibility of at least one more 25bp hike later this year with four penciling in two, Chair Warsh again declined to submit his forecasts, the SEP median is 4.1% for year-end, PCE inflation is projected at 3.7% for 2026 with core at 3.4%, GDP at 2.3% and unemployment at 4.1% in both 2026 and 2027. What changed in the last twenty-four hours is the front of the curve, not the Committee's direction. Tuesday's core PCE printed 0.2% m/m against a 0.3% forecast, the y/y rate came in at 3.0% against 3.3% expected, and headline was 3.4% against 3.7% - a genuinely soft report that sits below the Committee's own 3.4% core projection for the year. Final GDP was revised up to 2.2% annualised from 1.5%, and ADP came in at 90K against a 73K forecast and 36K previous, so the activity side of the same week was firm. John Williams then supplied the words that did the repricing, pushing back on an imminent follow-up and saying there is 'no urgency' after September's move while still seeing one more hike as potentially appropriate later this year. The others leaned the other way: Goolsbee said inflation staying above target for five and a half years is 'playing with fire' and that the Fed may need to respond, and Barkin indicated more hikes are likely needed. Cook and Kashkari also spoke. The honest summary is that the Committee has been repriced from October to December rather than from hiking to holding, which is why this entry stays on hike and the dollar stays at +2 - and why DXY rose 0.18% to 101.651 on the day it happened, with the ten-year up at 5.2820. The domestic data behind the stance is still the strongest here: September PMIs at 57.0 manufacturing and 58.7 services with non-manufacturing at 55.4, retail sales +1.2% m/m, headline CPI 3.4% with core 2.4%. Against it, the labour side is the soft spot - consumer confidence 48.1 from 51.7 and Friday's payroll forecast cut to 89K from 162K with unemployment at 4.1%, exactly the level the SEP carries across its whole horizon. A print at or below 89K with soft earnings makes December a real question too; a beat puts October back in play within a day. Note for completeness that the FY2027 continuing resolution was signed, funding agencies through December 11, so there is no shutdown risk to Friday's release.

EUR.when: October 29, with the decision at 14:15 CET from the October 28-29 meeting. Direction unchanged and the pace still measured: Lagarde has ruled out reacting to energy, so neither a 3.7% flash on Friday nor a gas price moving in either direction changes this path much. September meeting accounts land October 8
EUR.note: TE re-verified: the ECB deposit facility rate is 2.50%, raised from 2.25% in September, with the main refinancing rate at 2.65%. TE's summary describes it as the second hike since the US-Iran war began, with the ECB saying the conflict continues to fuel inflationary pressures and inflation expected to remain well above the 2% target for an extended period; the 2026 inflation forecast was kept at 3.0% with 2027 and 2028 revised up to 2.5% and 2.1%, growth upgraded to 0.9% for 2026 and 1.4% for 2027, and Lagarde saying at the press conference that growth risks are tilted to the downside while inflation risks are tilted to the upside, with decisions made meeting-by-meeting. The doctrine that governs this entry is unchanged and is still the most useful sentence on the page, from her ECON hearing on September 28: 'we do not react to energy prices, we react if we see risks of higher energy prices becoming embedded in inflation', with 'we do not see evidence at this stage of energy prices feeding into higher wages'. That cuts symmetrically, and today it cuts the other way from yesterday. Yesterday the euro gained because a reaction function that never responded to energy rising could not be damaged by energy falling; today energy has stopped falling, German gas is +4.09% in a session, and the same logic says the euro gains nothing back. This is why the euro holds +1 rather than extending - the score is relative, not earned. The inflation data is loud and still does not matter much: German CPI accelerated to 3.3% y/y in September from 2.9%, euro-area headline is 3.2% with core 2.4%, and Friday's flash at 09:00Z is forecast at 3.7% from 3.2% with core 2.5%. Her evidence on the wage channel holds - negotiated wage growth 2.44% from 2.56%, headline wage growth 3.0% from 3.4%. Activity is adequate: Q2 GDP 0.6% q/q and 1.2% y/y, unemployment 6.4%, employment +0.1% q/q. The word that would change this entry is any sign of 'embedded', which is the hatch she deliberately left open. Lagarde speaks today at 13:30Z.

GBP.when: November 5. Roughly 80% is still priced for 25bp from 3.75%, against a Reuters poll where about one in eight economists expected a hike. That gap is the trade in both directions, and it did not close today - it widened slightly as sterling rallied on the Q2 GDP revision
GBP.note: TE re-verified: Bank Rate is 3.75%. TE's summary of the September 16 meeting records a 6-3 vote to hold, with three members preferring 25bp to 4.00% - the same split as July. The MPC said prolonged Middle East conflict has pushed crude and refined energy prices higher and contributed to UK CPI rising to 3.1% in August, with further increases expected in coming quarters, and stressed that policy must return inflation sustainably to 2% while assessing the scale and duration of the energy shock; it noted limited evidence so far of significant second-round effects on wages and prices, with the risk rising if energy costs stay elevated. It also agreed unanimously to run the gilt stock to zero at an average £46 billion a year through 2034. This entry is where today's largest correction sits, and it should be stated plainly: yesterday this page cut sterling from +2 to 0 on the grounds that Bailey had made the stance conditional on energy and that both prices the Bank named on September 14 - Brent at 106 dollars and UK gas at 207 GBp/therm - had retreated. One of those two legs has partially reversed within a day. UK gas is 182.17 GBp/thm against the 175.26 quoted yesterday and is now +0.01% on the month rather than falling; German gas rose 4.09% in a session; Brent at 96.857 is +1.28% over four weeks. Meanwhile the UK produced the only positive growth revision on this board, Q2 GDP lifted to 1.4% y/y, and sterling rallied on it before giving back more than half. The gilt market agrees with the hawkish reading: the UK ten-year at 5.4148 is now the highest of the majors, above Australia's 5.3920. Breeden and Lombardelli have both been reported moving closer to backing a hike, which would turn 6-3 into something much closer. Sterling therefore returns to +1. It does not return to +2, because the asymmetry that justified part of yesterday's cut is genuinely unresolved - about 80% priced against roughly one in eight economists, with Bank of America expecting no change this year - and because the pound is still -1.76% on the month. CPI is 3.1% with core 2.6%, wage growth has cooled to 3.9% from 4.2%, unemployment is 4.9% and employment change +67k from +83k. Bailey speaks today at 08:00Z with Mann at 12:00Z, and the single thing to listen for is whether the energy condition is restated as a trigger or softened to a risk.

JPY.when: October 30 is still the scheduled meeting and comes with a Quarterly Outlook Report, but the Summary of Opinions published at 23:50Z damped the back-to-back case and the market has moved the likely move toward December or January. Tokyo core CPI tonight at 23:30Z, forecast 2.4% from 1.8%, is the near test
JPY.note: TE re-verified: the BoJ policy rate is 1.25%, raised 25bp in September on a 7-2 vote - the highest since April 1995. TE records that the split highlighted growing divisions over the pace of normalisation as the Bank responds to persistent inflation including higher oil prices, that most policymakers signalled support for further increases while Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato dissented, that the hike came just three months after the previous one - the shortest interval since 1990 - and that it followed pressure from Washington including calls from Treasury Secretary Bessent for higher rates. The Bank expects inflation above 2% in coming years with analysts seeing price growth near 3% by early next year. What changed overnight is the timing, and it changed because of the Bank's own publication rather than any data. The Summary of Opinions from the September 17-18 meeting was read as a refusal to pre-commit to October: the yen fell as much as 0.55% to 158.279 and was the worst G10 performer as investors cut back-to-back bets. The contents are more hawkish than that reaction suggests, which is exactly why this is a one-point cut and not a reversal. Members described a shift in the phase of policy from lifting inflation to stabilising it around 2%. One said that 'if signs of an upward deviation in prices are observed, the Bank will need to accelerate the pace of rate hikes'. Most favoured further increases. The dovish counterweights are real but narrow: the two named dissenters, and a Cabinet Office representative urging the Bank to examine carefully the cumulative effects of past hikes. The Tankan released the same morning pointed the same way, with large-manufacturer sentiment rising for a sixth consecutive quarter to plus 24 from plus 22 on AI-related demand, though it missed the plus 25 expected. The fundamentals under the yen remain the best on this board for a hawkish case: wage growth 4.7% y/y, the strongest here and the only credible second-round mechanism anywhere on this page; producer prices elevated; CPI 1.9% with core 1.7%; unemployment 2.4% and falling; a ten-year at 3.1010 that has repriced hard this year. Tokyo core CPI tonight at 23:30Z, forecast 2.4% against 1.8%, is the one print that could put October back in play within a session. Treat the 157-160 band defined by the July 31 joint intervention as official until the MoF says otherwise - spot at 158.279 sits inside it.

AUD.when: November 3 at 03:30Z, an hour earlier after the October 3 daylight-saving shift. The trigger for a follow-up went when the trimmed mean cooled to 0.2% m/m, and most economists already had 4.60% as the peak. The September-quarter CPI in late October is the print that decides it
AUD.note: TE re-verified: the cash rate is 4.60%, raised 25bp unanimously in September - the fourth hike of 2026 and the highest since 2011. TE records the Board naming higher global energy prices from oil supply disruptions amid the Middle East conflict, stronger-than-expected recent inflation and persistent domestic capacity constraints as adding to inflation, with AI-related demand driving global technology goods prices and firms reporting rising costs and plans to pass them on; output growth slowed but was slightly stronger than expected in Q2, consumer spending is easing, housing prices fell in most capital cities and new housing loans declined, and labour market conditions have now also eased. The Board said further tightening may be needed to prevent inflation becoming embedded. Australia holds at 0 and the reason is that it is genuinely balanced rather than quiet. On the hawkish side: the highest policy rate on this board by 85bp over Bank Rate, a 5.3920 ten-year that is second only to the UK, headline CPI at 4.0% y/y from 3.5%, a trimmed mean stuck at 3.6% for a third month, and a Board that has used the word embedded. On the dovish side: last week's CPI came in below forecast on all three measures with the trimmed mean at 0.2% m/m against 0.3%, unemployment has risen to 4.6% from 4.5%, GDP growth has decelerated to 2.1% y/y from 2.5%, wage growth is flat at 3.2%, and the quarterly y/y rate eased to 3.9% from 4.1%. The energy argument the Board explicitly hiked into has become ambiguous rather than reversed - crude is lower but gas is higher - and in any case Australia is a net energy exporter, so the channel cuts both ways. AUD/USD at 0.69433 is -3.15% on the month and has not managed to hold 0.70 on any dollar-negative session this week, which is the market's own verdict on the long leg. Copper, its other tie, is flat at 6.5541 into a Chinese Golden Week that started today.

NZD.when: October 28, a Monetary Policy Review without a full statement. Widely expected to hold at 2.75%, with TE's own projection carrying 3.00% by December 9. The Bank has already framed Q2's 4.1% as largely fuel-driven, which is the language of a central bank preparing to look through a print
NZD.note: TE re-verified: the official cash rate is 2.75%, raised 25bp in September - a second straight hike after July. TE records the decision as reflecting the need to gradually remove monetary stimulus and return inflation to the 2% midpoint while supporting growth and employment; annual inflation rose to 4.1% in Q2 largely on higher fuel prices from the Middle East conflict, but core inflation, wage growth and inflation expectations remain consistent with inflation returning to the 1-3% band by mid-2027. The economy has likely resumed its recovery after lacklustre Q2 growth, supported by resilient external demand, export prices and investment in export-oriented sectors, while weak income growth, job insecurity and flat house prices weigh on household spending and residential investment. New Zealand stays at -1 and stays the weakest major on the month, with NZD/USD at 0.56193 down 3.94% over four weeks - the worst of the eight. The domestic evidence got slightly worse rather than better: business confidence fell to 51.9 from 53.7 and building permits to 3,339 units from 3,487. Underneath that, wage growth at 2.1% is the lowest on this board and unemployment at 5.6% is the highest, which together are precisely why the Bank can look through a 4.1% headline it has already attributed to fuel. The fuel in question is no longer falling as fast - crude is down but gas is up - which removes a little of yesterday's incremental dovishness without changing the level. The ten-year at 5.1140 is the lowest of the antipodeans. Against all of this, the kiwi is cheap and heavily sold, which is the main risk to holding shorts here: an October 28 review with firmer language would hurt, and TE's projection of 3.00% by December says the tightening cycle is not formally over.

CAD.when: October 28, with the Monetary Policy Report. OIS was close to a coin flip in late September and most bank economists already expected no move in 2026; July GDP at 0.0% m/m pushed it toward hold. The Business Outlook Survey on October 19 is the earlier read
CAD.note: TE re-verified: the overnight rate is 2.25%, held in September. TE records the Governing Council noting a broad recovery in the Canadian economy in Q2, underscoring some resilience since the war in the Middle East lifted energy prices and long-maturity domestic yields, while flagging stronger upside inflation risks from the continuation of the war and the reintroduction of aggressive tariffs on Canadian exports to the United States; the Bank also noted that underlying inflation has so far maintained its target level despite the energy shock, and reiterated that the uncertain outlook prevents clear signals on policy this year. Canada stays at -1 with nothing to revise, and it is the one currency on this board whose case rests on domestic data rather than on the energy story. July GDP printed 0.0% m/m with manufacturing -0.9% and mining, quarrying and oil and gas -0.5%, after three months of expansion, with the August flash at +0.2%. The services PMI at 46.8 and the composite at 47.8 remain the only contracting readings anywhere on this page, and they deteriorated from 49.1 and 49.7. Inflation gives the Bank no reason to move either: headline 3.0% y/y, the monthly rate negative at -0.1%, core 2.4%. Employment fell 41.7k in August after +75.1k, unemployment is 6.4%, wage growth has eased to 3.2% from 3.39%. The terms-of-trade leg is still working against the loonie with WTI at 89.046 and -5.88% on the week, and Macklem has already said the Bank must look beyond the initial shock of higher oil prices. USD/CAD at 1.42472 is +2.93% on the month and the three-point score gap to the dollar is the widest clean policy divergence on the board. What would change this entry is a Gulf re-escalation that restores the terms-of-trade bid, or a Business Outlook Survey on October 19 that shows the PMIs overstating the weakness.

CHF.when: December 10, with the press release at 09:30 CET and the news conference at 10:00. Nothing in the Bank's own two-year forecast requires a move in either direction, and five consecutive meetings at zero is now the base case for a sixth. CPI this morning at 06:30Z and Schlegel at 15:30Z are the near events
CHF.note: TE re-verified: the SNB policy rate is 0.00%, held in September and unchanged since mid-2025. TE records policymakers saying the current stance remains appropriate to maintain price stability and support economic development, with inflation having risen to 0.8% in August from 0.6% in May driven mainly by higher energy prices; the SNB expects inflation to rise further in Q4 before easing through 2027, and forecasts average inflation of 0.7% in 2026 and 0.8% in both 2027 and 2028. It projects GDP growth of 1.5-2% in 2026 and around 1.5% in 2027 while highlighting high uncertainty from Middle East tensions, global growth, trade policy and exchange rates, and says it remains willing to intervene in foreign exchange markets as necessary. The franc stays at -2 and remains the weakest currency on this board, for the structural reason that nothing here has moved in five meetings and nothing in the Bank's own forecast asks it to. Core inflation is 0.4%, wage growth is 0.4% - both the lowest on this page by a wide margin - and the ten-year at 0.5690 is a fraction of every other yield here, which is the entire carry case against it. The important observation is behavioural rather than numerical: the haven bid has now failed to arrive on escalation days and on de-escalation days alike, which is what makes the CHF short leg usable in size rather than only in direction. USD/CHF at 0.83655 is +2.91% on the month. The honest risk is that the SNB's historical sensitivity to franc strength cuts both ways, and that the entire rise in Swiss inflation to 0.8% was energy, so a genuine re-escalation would lift the print and the currency at once. CPI at 06:30Z this morning is forecast at 0.0% m/m against 0.4% - a flat print confirms there is no domestic Swiss inflation to respond to at all - and Schlegel speaks at 15:30Z, where the only thing that matters is whether he hardens back toward intervention after September's softening to acting only as necessary.

strength.tag: Held at +2 while the October hike was priced out, because December is unchanged at about 90% and the dollar rose anyway
strength.drivers: TE re-verified: fed funds upper bound 4.00%, headline CPI 3.4% with core 2.4%, unemployment 4.1%, August NFP +162k, Q2 GDP revised up to 2.2% annualised from 1.5%. September PMIs are the strongest on this board at 57.0 manufacturing, 58.7 services and 55.4 non-manufacturing, retail sales +1.2% m/m, and ADP beat at 90K against a 73K forecast. The ten-year rose to 5.2820 for a real yield near 2.88%, and DXY gained 0.18% to 101.651, now +2.06% on the month. Against that, Tuesday's core PCE printed 0.2% m/m against 0.3% with the y/y rate at 3.0% against 3.3% expected and headline 3.4% against 3.7%, consumer confidence has fallen to 48.1 from 51.7, and Friday's payroll forecast is 89K from 162K.
strength.forward: 🦅 Still the hawkish side of this board into December 9, held at +2, and the reason for holding rather than cutting again is a distinction the headlines skipped. The October 27-28 hike has genuinely been priced out: CME FedWatch is 47.1% hike against 52.9% hold, one read is as low as 37%, and Kalshi and Polymarket are near 35%, against 69-73% before the core PCE print. John Williams did it with words rather than data, pushing back on an imminent follow-up and saying there is 'no urgency' after September's move. But the cumulative curve did not move: the probability of the funds rate being unchanged through December 9 is only about 10%, with 51.8% priced for a cumulative 25bp and 38.2% for 50bp. That is a market moving a hike one meeting to the right, not abandoning it - and Williams himself still sees one more as potentially appropriate later this year, Goolsbee said five and a half years above target is 'playing with fire' and the Fed may need to respond, Barkin indicated more hikes are likely needed, and the September SEP has 16 of 18 officials seeing at least one more 25bp this year with a 4.1% year-end median against today's 4.00%. The tape is the strongest single argument here: a currency repriced dovish at the front that still gains 0.18% on the day, sits +2.06% on the month, and does it while its own ten-year rises to 5.2820, is being held for carry and for the absence of alternatives - and the alternatives are what deteriorated overnight, with the BoJ damping its own October move. What invalidates +2 is Friday's payroll at or materially below the 89K forecast with soft average hourly earnings, which would start pricing December out too and take the dollar to +1; what restores a case for +3 is a beat with firm earnings, which puts October back in play inside a session. Note that the FY2027 continuing resolution has been signed through December 11, so unlike earlier episodes this release is not at risk of being delayed.

strength.tag: Raised from 0 back to +1: yesterday's cut over-read one session of energy relief, and UK gas, UK growth and the gilt have all since gone the other way
strength.drivers: TE re-verified: Bank Rate 3.75% after a 6-3 hold on September 16 with three members preferring 4.00%, headline CPI 3.1% with core 2.6%, unemployment 4.9%, employment change +67k from +83k, wage growth cooled to 3.9% from 4.2%. Q2 GDP was revised up to 1.4% y/y - the only positive growth revision on this board - and the ten-year at 5.4148 is now the highest of the majors, above Australia's 5.3920. UK gas has reversed to 182.17 GBp/thm from the 175.26 this page quoted yesterday and is +0.01% on the month, while Brent at 96.857 is +1.28% over four weeks. Roughly 80% remains priced for November 5. GBP/USD at 1.32490 is -0.12% on the day and -1.76% on the month.
strength.forward: 🦅 Hawkish-leaning into November 5, raised from 0 to +1, and the honest framing is that this is a correction of yesterday's own call rather than new information. Yesterday this page cut sterling two points on the argument that Bailey had made the stance explicitly conditional on high energy - 'it's going to get harder to maintain that stance the longer we have high energy prices' - and that both prices the Bank named on September 14, Brent at 106 dollars and UK gas at 207 GBp/therm, had retreated. One of those two legs reversed inside twenty-four hours. UK gas is back to 182.17 GBp/thm and is now flat on the month rather than falling, German gas rose 4.09% in a single session, and Brent is positive over four weeks. A thesis built on a one-day energy move was too fast, and this entry says so. What has arrived since is all on the hawkish side: the Q2 GDP revision to 1.4% y/y is the only positive growth revision anywhere on this board and sterling rallied on it before giving back more than half; the gilt market has taken the UK ten-year to 5.4148, the highest yield of the majors; three MPC members already vote for 4.00%, and Breeden and Lombardelli have been reported moving closer to joining them, which would turn 6-3 into a near-tie. The reason this is +1 rather than a return to +2 is that the asymmetry remains genuinely unresolved and is still the most interesting thing about sterling: about 80% is priced for a November hike against a Reuters poll in which roughly one in eight economists expected one, with Bank of America expecting no change this year. Wage growth cooling to 3.9% from 4.2% is the Bank's own best evidence that second-round effects are not building, and the MPC said as much. So the pound is a hold-and-watch rather than a conviction long: the single cleanest test arrives today at 08:00Z when Bailey speaks, with Mann at 12:00Z. If the energy condition is restated as a hard trigger with gas back above 180, sterling goes to +2 and EUR/GBP becomes a short; if it is softened to one risk among several, the 80% pricing starts unwinding and the case for yesterday's 0 returns.

strength.tag: Cut from +2 to +1: the BoJ's own Summary of Opinions damped the October back-to-back hike and the yen was the worst G10 performer
strength.drivers: TE re-verified: the BoJ policy rate is 1.25% after a 7-2 hike in September, the highest since April 1995, with Asada and Sato dissenting and most policymakers signalling support for further increases. Wage growth is 4.7% y/y, the strongest on this board; CPI 1.9% with core 1.7%; unemployment 2.4% and falling; the ten-year at 3.1010. The Summary of Opinions published at 23:50Z was read as a refusal to pre-commit to October 30, and the yen fell as much as 0.55% to 158.279, the worst of the G10. The Tankan rose for a sixth consecutive quarter to plus 24 from plus 22 on AI-related demand, missing the plus 25 expected. USD/JPY is -0.27% on the month and sits inside the 157-160 band the July 31 joint intervention defined.
strength.forward: 🦅 Still the hawkish side of the carry trade into October 30, but cut from +2 to +1, and this page should own the sequence: yesterday it raised the yen two points, and the Bank of Japan's own publication took one of them back within a session. The Summary of Opinions from the September 17-18 meeting landed at 23:50Z and the market read it as a refusal rather than a signal - the yen fell as much as 0.55% to 158.279 and was the worst G10 performer as investors cut bets on a back-to-back hike on October 30. The contents are more hawkish than that price action implies, which is precisely why one point comes off and not two. Members described a shift in the phase of policy from lifting inflation to stabilising it around 2%, which is the language of a bank that thinks the job is nearly normal rather than nearly done. One member said that 'if signs of an upward deviation in prices are observed, the Bank will need to accelerate the pace of rate hikes'. Most favoured further increases. The dovish counterweights are narrow and already known: Asada and Sato, plus a Cabinet Office representative urging the Bank to examine carefully the cumulative effects of past hikes. The Tankan the same morning rose for a sixth straight quarter. So the direction is unchanged and the fundamental set is still the best hawkish case on this board - 4.7% wage growth is the only credible second-round mechanism on this page, against a Bank that has just delivered its shortest interval between hikes since 1990. What a currency cannot do is hold +2 while it is the worst performer in its peer group and its next move has been pushed from four weeks away to twelve. The cleanest near test is Tokyo core CPI tonight at 23:30Z, forecast 2.4% against 1.8% previous: a print at or above forecast puts October 30 back in play inside a session and argues for restoring +2, while a miss confirms the market's reading and would take the yen toward 0 alongside a retest of the upper half of the intervention band. Hold 157-160 as official until the MoF says otherwise, and note that spot at 158.279 is now in the middle of it rather than at either edge.

strength.tag: Unchanged at +1 on a case that is purely relative - the energy-blindness that paid the euro yesterday stops paying it now that energy has stopped falling
strength.drivers: TE re-verified: the ECB deposit facility rate is 2.50% with the main refinancing rate at 2.65%, after the second hike since the US-Iran war began. Headline inflation 3.2% y/y with core 2.4%, Q2 GDP 0.6% q/q and 1.2% y/y, unemployment 6.4%, employment +0.1% q/q. German CPI accelerated to 3.3% y/y in September from 2.9%, and Friday's euro-area flash is forecast at 3.7% from 3.2% with core 2.5%. Negotiated wage growth is 2.44% from 2.56% and headline wage growth 3.0% from 3.4%, both decelerating. The Bund yields 3.5787 against France at 4.8450 and Italy at 4.6400. EUR/USD at 1.13173 is -0.11% on the day and -2.34% on the month.
strength.forward: ⚖️ Balanced into October 29, held at +1, and MIXED rather than STRENGTHENING because the score is relative and the price action says so - a currency that is -2.34% on the month is not strengthening in any observable sense. The doctrine is unchanged and remains the most useful sentence available on the euro, from Lagarde's ECON hearing on September 28: 'we do not react to energy prices, we react if we see risks of higher energy prices becoming embedded in inflation', with 'we do not see evidence at this stage of energy prices feeding into higher wages'. The point to make today is that this cuts symmetrically, and yesterday this page only used one side of it. Yesterday the euro was raised because a reaction function that never responded to energy rising could not be damaged by energy falling, while sterling, the loonie and the kiwi handed back premium. Energy has now stopped falling - German gas +4.09% in a session, UK gas flat on the month, Brent +1.28% over four weeks - so that relative gain stops accruing, and the honest consequence is that the euro holds its point without earning another. The inflation data this week is loud and still buys nothing: German CPI at 3.3% from 2.9% and a 3.7% euro-area flash forecast for Friday are, on the ECB's own stated reaction function, a growth negative rather than a policy positive, and negotiated wages decelerating to 2.44% are the evidence Lagarde cites for why. Growth is adequate rather than good and the periphery spread is the quiet risk nobody is pricing: France at 4.8450 against the Bund at 3.5787 is a 127bp gap, which is why EU50 carries French and Italian political risk that the DAX does not. Trade the euro in crosses rather than against the dollar, and with lower conviction than yesterday: EUR/GBP has already gone from a flip-to-long to a range as sterling recovered its point, which is the clearest illustration that this score is borrowed from other currencies' weakness rather than owned. What would make it genuinely strengthening is the word 'embedded' appearing in Lagarde's remarks today at 13:30Z, or a Friday flash that beats 3.7% with core above 2.5% on something other than fuel.

strength.tag: Unchanged at 0 and genuinely two-sided: the highest policy rate on this board against a rising unemployment rate and a pair that cannot hold 0.70
strength.drivers: TE re-verified: the cash rate is 4.60% after a unanimous 25bp hike in September, the fourth of 2026 and the highest since 2011, with the Board saying further tightening may be needed to prevent inflation becoming embedded. Headline CPI 4.0% y/y from 3.5%, core 3.6%, the quarterly y/y rate easing to 3.9% from 4.1%; unemployment risen to 4.6% from 4.5%, GDP decelerating to 2.1% y/y from 2.5%, wage growth flat at 3.2%, employment +39.5k. The ten-year at 5.3920 is second only to the UK. Last week's monthly CPI came in below forecast on all three measures with the trimmed mean at 0.2% m/m against 0.3%. AUD/USD at 0.69433 is -0.06% on the day and -3.15% on the month. Copper is flat at 6.5541.
strength.forward: ⚖️ Range into November 3, held at 0, and this is a balanced score rather than an absent one - both sides are substantial and they genuinely offset. The hawkish side: the highest policy rate on this board by 85bp over Bank Rate, a 5.3920 ten-year, a headline CPI that accelerated to 4.0% y/y, a trimmed mean that has now been stuck at 3.6% for a third consecutive month, and a Board that used the word 'embedded' in its own September statement while naming higher global energy prices, stronger-than-expected inflation and persistent domestic capacity constraints. The dovish side: last week's monthly CPI undershot forecast on all three measures, with the trimmed mean at 0.2% m/m against 0.3% - which removed the trigger for a November follow-up - and the domestic picture has softened, with unemployment up to 4.6%, growth decelerating to 2.1% y/y, flat 3.2% wages, housing prices falling in most capital cities, and the RBA itself acknowledging that labour market conditions have now also eased. The energy argument deserves care, because yesterday this page cut the Aussie partly on an energy unwind that has since stalled. The right conclusion is not to put the point back but to note that the channel has become ambiguous: crude is lower, gas is higher, and Australia is a net energy exporter so the transmission runs the opposite way to Japan's in the first place. The market's verdict is the most informative single fact here: on a week in which the dollar's October hike was priced out, AUD/USD still could not hold 0.70 and is -3.15% over four weeks. A pair that will not rally when its short leg is being marked down is telling you the long leg is the problem. The real gate is the September-quarter CPI in late October, which decides November 3; before that, copper is the tie worth watching, flat at 6.5541 into a Chinese Golden Week that began today and with 2026 demand growth running at 2.3% against 4.1% last year. A quarterly trimmed mean back above 1.0% q/q takes AUD to +1; a further rise in unemployment takes it to -1.

strength.forward: 🔻 Dovish-leaning into October 28, held at -1, and Canada is now the one currency on this board whose score rests on domestic data rather than on the energy narrative - which is exactly why it did not need revising today when the energy narrative stalled. The domestic case is unambiguous and it is the weakest set of readings on this page. July GDP at 0.0% m/m ended three months of expansion, with the goods-producing side leading the stall. The services PMI at 46.8 and the composite at 47.8 are the only sub-50 readings anywhere on this board and they deteriorated from 49.1 and 49.7, so the direction is wrong as well as the level. Inflation offers the Bank no reason to act in either direction: headline is 3.0% y/y, the monthly rate is actually negative at -0.1%, and core at 2.4% is inside the band - which is precisely what the Bank meant when it said underlying inflation has so far maintained its target level despite the energy shock since March. The terms-of-trade leg is still working against the loonie rather than for it, with WTI at 89.046 and -5.88% on the week, and that is the one place where today's stalled energy move matters: gas rising does nothing for Canada, because Canada's export is crude. strength.drivers: TE re-verified: the official cash rate is 2.75% after a second straight 25bp hike in September, with the Bank saying core inflation, wage growth and inflation expectations remain consistent with a return to the 1-3% band by mid-2027 despite Q2 inflation rising to 4.1% largely on higher fuel prices. Wage growth at 2.1% is the lowest on this board and unemployment at 5.6% the highest; core inflation 3.2%; GDP 2.6% y/y with the quarterly rate slowing to 0.2% from 0.9%; employment +0.5% q/q. Business confidence fell to 51.9 from 53.7 and building permits to 3,339 units from 3,487. The ten-year at 5.1140 is the lowest of the antipodeans. strength.forward: 🔻 Dovish-leaning into October 28, held at -1, and the case is the same one it has been for a fortnight: a central bank that has pre-committed to looking through its own headline inflation print, and the labour data that lets it. The Bank's September language did the work - annual inflation at 4.1% in Q2 attributed largely to higher fuel prices from the Middle East conflict, with core inflation, wage growth and expectations all described as consistent with a return to the 1-3% band by mid-2027. Underneath that, wage growth at 2.1% is the lowest number on this board and unemployment at 5.6% the highest, and together they are a complete answer to anyone arguing that a 4.1% print forces a response. Today's incremental news went the same way: business confidence fell to 51.9 from 53.7 and building permits to 3,339 units from 3,487, so the domestic recovery the Bank says it expects to strengthen and broaden is not yet visible in the forward indicators. The quarterly growth rate has also slowed to 0.2% from 0.9% even as the annual rate rose to 2.6%. One thing deserves flagging rather than ignoring: yesterday the kiwi's remaining hawkish tail was described as thinner because fuel was falling, and fuel has partly stopped falling - crude is lower but gas is higher. That does not change the level, because New Zealand's inflation problem was petrol rather than gas, but it does mean the incremental dovishness claimed yesterday should not be claimed again. The honest risk to holding kiwi shorts is positioning rather than fundamentals: at -3.94% on the month this is the most heavily sold major on the board, TE's own projection still carries 3.00% by December 9, and the October 28 Monetary Policy Review is a lower-information event than a full statement, which makes a hawkish surprise cheaper to deliver. Firmer language on October 28, or a Q3 CPI that shows core rather than fuel driving the print, takes NZD back to 0.

Headline inflation is 0.8% y/y, driven mainly by energy, with core at 0.4% and wage growth at 0.4% - both the lowest on this board by a wide margin. The SNB's own forecast is 0.7% average inflation in 2026 and 0.8% in both 2027 and 2028, with GDP growth of 1.5-2% in 2026. Unemployment 3.0%, employment +0.5% q/q, Q2 GDP 2.3% y/y. strength.forward: 🔻 Dovish by construction into December 10, held at -2, and the franc remains the most useful short leg on this board for a reason that is structural rather than tactical: nothing here has changed in five consecutive meetings and nothing in the Bank's own two-year forecast asks it to. Core inflation at 0.4% and wage growth at 0.4% are the lowest numbers on this page by a wide margin, the entire rise in headline inflation to 0.8% was energy by the SNB's own description, and a policy rate of exactly zero against a ten-year of 0.5690 means every other currency here is paid to be long against it - 400bp from the dollar, 460bp from the Aussie, 375bp from sterling. The observation worth adding today is behavioural rather than numerical, and it is what justifies using the franc short in size rather than only in direction: the haven bid has now failed to arrive on escalation days, when the strait was being threatened and a naval blockade was in force, and it has failed to arrive on de-escalation days, when a Saudi supply recovery and a Qatari-mediated counterproposal were the headlines. The BoC is expected to hold at 2.25% after July GDP printed 0.0%; the RBNZ is widely expected to hold at 2.75% though TE still projects 3.00% by December 9. The UK Budget lands the same day.

catalysts.event: ECB Governing Council decision
catalysts.note: Decision at 14:15 CET from the October 28-29 meeting, with the deposit rate at 2.50%. Direction is still a hike but the pace is measured and pre-announced as energy-blind, which makes this a lower-variance event than the others in the cluster - and the reason the euro's +1 is a borrowed score rather than an earned one. September meeting accounts land October 8.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan decision with Quarterly Outlook Report
catalysts.note: The meeting the Summary of Opinions has just damped, and still the biggest scheduled risk to the JPY score in both directions. Most members favoured further hikes and one said the Bank must accelerate if prices deviate upward, but two dovish dissents and a Cabinet Office request to examine the cumulative effects of past hikes argue for a pause. An Outlook Report is where the BoJ revises its inflation path, which is why this matters more than a bare decision.

catalysts.event: RBA Cash Rate decision
catalysts.note: At 03:30Z, an hour earlier after the October 3 daylight-saving shift. The trigger for a follow-up went when the trimmed mean cooled to 0.2% m/m, and most economists already had 4.60% as the peak. The September-quarter CPI in late October is the print that actually decides it.

catalysts.event: Bank of England decision
catalysts.note: The meeting today's sterling upgrade is about. Roughly 80% is priced for 25bp from 3.75% after a 6-3 hold where three members already preferred 4.00%, against a Reuters poll in which about one in eight economists expected a hike and Bank of America expecting no change this year. Breeden and Lombardelli have been reported moving closer to backing a hike. That unresolved gap is why sterling is +1 rather than +2.

catalysts.event: FOMC decision - now the live meeting for the dollar
catalysts.note: With October repriced to the mid-30s to 47%, this is where the Fed's next move is actually priced: only about 10% for the funds rate being unchanged through this date, with 51.8% for a cumulative 25bp and 38.2% for 50bp. Williams has said he still sees one more hike as potentially appropriate later this year. The December 11 funding deadline arrives two days later.

catalysts.event: SNB quarterly monetary policy assessment
catalysts.note: Press release 09:30 CET and news conference 10:00. The policy rate has been at 0.00% for five meetings and nothing in the Bank's own two-year forecast - 0.7% average inflation in 2026 and 0.8% in 2027 and 2028 - requires a move in either direction. The near-term question is not this meeting but whether Schlegel hardens the intervention language before it.

catalysts.event: Iran / US talks and the Strait of Hormuz, plus the Saudi export recovery
catalysts.note: Still the variable that sets every energy-conditional policy path on this board, and it advanced on diplomacy this week rather than only on supply. Iran confirmed on September 30 that it received Washington's response to its seven-day reopening proposal through Qatari mediators, with the remaining gap over sequencing: Tehran wants an end to military and economic pressure, frozen assets released and a safe shipping route, while Washington prefers to address the nuclear file simultaneously. Trump rejected the original plan outright. The strait remains closed and the naval blockade remains in force.

catalysts.event: China Golden Week from October 1 and the copper physical market
catalysts.note: The week-long holiday began today, which thins the physical bid and makes this week's copper prints low-information. Underneath it the supply story is still tight and demand is still structural through AI and grid build-out, against 2026 demand growth of 2.3% versus 4.1% last year. Tied to AUD, which is scored 0 - a copper breakout after the restart is the most likely route to taking the Aussie to +1.

catalysts.event: US federal funding deadline under the FY2027 continuing resolution
catalysts.note: Worth carrying because it removes a risk rather than creates one near term: the continuing resolution signed for fiscal 2027 funds agencies through December 11, 2026, which is why Friday's payroll release is not in question. It does, however, land two days after the December 9 FOMC that now carries the dollar's next move.

geopolitics: The energy transmission channel split in two this week, and keeping the halves separate is the most practically useful thing on this page. On crude, the direction is still down and the reasons are now both physical and diplomatic. The physical leg is the Saudi export recovery confirmed by satellite imagery at the Yanbu and Muajjiz terminals on the Red Sea - a route that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz entirely - with Middle East crude exports estimated near 98% of pre-war levels. The diplomatic leg advanced on September 30, when Iran confirmed it had received Washington's response to its seven-day Hormuz reopening proposal through Qatari mediators. Foreign Minister Araghchi's delegation had delivered what he called a concrete plan at the UN General Assembly, under which normal maritime passage could be restored within seven days if conditions were met; the remaining disagreement is reported to be over sequencing rather than substance. Tehran's conditions are an end to American military and economic pressure, the release of frozen assets and agreement on a safe shipping route, while Washington prefers to address the nuclear file at the same time as Hormuz. Trump rejected the original Iranian plan outright, saying a deal that reopened the strait immediately would not be acceptable. So the strait is still closed, the naval blockade reimposed in August is still in force, and what has changed is that a counterproposal now exists - which is why WTI is 89.046 and -5.88% on the week rather than why it has collapsed. On European gas, the direction has reversed, and this is the part that corrects yesterday's page. German gas rose 4.09% in a single session to 73.58 EUR/MWh and is +3.85% on the month; UK gas is back to 182.17 GBp/thm from the 175.26 quoted here yesterday and is now flat over four weeks; Brent at 96.857 is +1.28% on the month even as WTI falls. Gas is trading storage and weather, crude is trading Hormuz, and they have genuinely decoupled. The FX consequence is specific. Yesterday every energy-conditional hawkish case on this board was described as watching its own trigger retreat, and sterling was cut two points on exactly that reasoning. One session later the UK gas price the Bank of England itself named has gone back up, so sterling returns to +1 and the EUR/GBP long flipped on yesterday is withdrawn. Canada is unaffected by the correction because Canada exports crude rather than gas, so it stays at -1 on a terms-of-trade leg that is still working against it plus the worst domestic data on the board. Japan, the purest energy importer here, keeps the import-bill relief but loses the point it was given for it, because the BoJ's own Summary of Opinions - not the oil price - damped the October hike that the upgrade was predicated on. The euro keeps its relative point without earning another, since a reaction function Lagarde has declared energy-blind in both directions cannot be paid again for energy that has stopped moving its way. Australia, a net energy exporter, is indifferent in both directions and stays at 0. And the franc stays at -2 on the observation that matters most for sizing the six CHF longs on this page: the haven bid failed to arrive when the strait was being threatened, and it failed to arrive when it was being negotiated. The reversal risk to all of this is unchanged and it is sharp rather than gradual - a strike on the restored Saudi infrastructure, or a harder closure, would reprice crude faster than any central bank could respond, and would do it with the Fed's October meeting already priced below a coin flip.
